title: My New Bike
text: I got a new bike for my birthday. It is a blue bike with a small bell. Every morning I ride the bike to school. The school is near a park, so I ride through the park. I see a lot of birds there. After school, I ride home with a friend. It is the best present I have ever had.

title: The Bakery
text: There is a bakery on the corner of my street. The owner is an old man with a big smile. He opens the shop at six o'clock every morning. I usually buy a loaf of bread and an apple pie. The pie is warm and sweet. On Sundays, the bakery is very busy, and there is a long line outside the door.

title: A Rainy Day
text: It was a rainy day, so we stayed at home. My brother read a book about the ocean. I made a cake with my mother. The kitchen smelled of chocolate. In the afternoon, we watched a movie on the sofa. When the rain stopped, we saw a rainbow over the hill. It was a quiet but happy day.

title: My Cat, Mimi
text: I have a cat called Mimi. She is a white cat with green eyes. Mimi sleeps on the sofa for most of the day. At night, she likes to sit by the window and watch the moon. She is afraid of the vacuum cleaner. When I come home, she runs to the door. She is a funny and friendly animal.

title: At the Beach
text: Last summer, my family went to the beach. The sand was hot, and the sea was cold. My sister found an orange shell near the water. My father built a sandcastle with a tall tower. We ate sandwiches under a big umbrella. In the evening, the sun went down behind an island. I want to go there again next year.

title: The Lost Umbrella
text: Yesterday I lost my umbrella on the bus. It was a red umbrella with white spots. I called the bus company, and a woman answered the phone. She asked me for the number of the bus. The next day, I went to the office. The umbrella was on a shelf with a lot of other lost things. I was very happy.

title: Breakfast
text: Every day I eat breakfast at seven o'clock. I usually have an egg, a piece of toast, and a glass of milk. My father drinks a cup of coffee and reads the news on his phone. My little sister eats a banana. On the weekend, we have a big breakfast together at the table. It is my favourite meal of the day.

title: A New Student
text: A new student came to our class today. Her name is Sora, and she is from Busan. The teacher gave her a desk next to the window. At lunch, I sat with her in the cafeteria. She told me about the sea in her city. She has a dog and a hamster. I think she will be a good friend.

title: The Library
text: I go to the library every Saturday. It is a big building in the centre of the town. On the first floor, there is a room for children. I like the second floor because it is quiet. I usually borrow a comic book and a novel. The librarian is a kind woman, and she always helps me find an interesting book.

title: Shopping for Shoes
text: My old shoes had a hole in them, so I went to the mall with my mother. The shoe shop was on the third floor. I tried on a pair of black shoes, but they were too small. Then I found an excellent pair of white sneakers. They were the right size. My mother paid at the counter, and we went home.

title: A Day at the Zoo
text:
On Saturday, my class went to the zoo. We took a bus from the school, and the trip was about an hour long. When we arrived, our teacher gave each of us a map.

First, we went to see the elephants. There was a baby elephant with its mother. The baby was playing in the water and splashing everyone. Next, we visited the monkeys. One monkey took a hat from a boy and ran up a tree. Everybody laughed, but the boy was not happy.

At noon, we had lunch in a small park inside the zoo. I ate a sandwich and an orange. After lunch, we saw a tiger sleeping under a tree. It was the biggest cat I have ever seen.

In the afternoon, we bought a postcard at the gift shop. On the bus home, I fell asleep. It was a long day, but it was a lot of fun.

title: My Grandmother's Garden
text:
My grandmother lives in a small house in the country. Behind the house, there is a beautiful garden. She works in the garden every morning, even in the winter.

In the spring, she plants a lot of vegetables. She grows potatoes, carrots, and an unusual kind of purple cabbage. There is also an apple tree in the corner of the garden. In the autumn, the tree is full of red apples, and we pick them together.

When I visit her, she gives me a small basket. I walk around the garden and collect tomatoes and beans. Then we cook dinner in the kitchen with the vegetables from the garden. The food always tastes better than the food from the supermarket.

My grandmother says that a garden is like a friend. You have to visit it often and take care of it. I want to have a garden like hers one day.

title: The School Festival
text:
Every year, our school has a festival in October. It is the most exciting day of the year for the students.

This year, my class had a food stall. We sold rice cakes and hot chocolate. My friend Minho wore a chef's hat and an apron. He shouted, "Delicious rice cakes! Only a thousand won!" A lot of people came to our stall, and we sold everything before lunch.

In the afternoon, there was a talent show in the gym. A girl from the third grade sang a song, and a boy played the guitar. Our music teacher did a magic trick with a rabbit. The audience cheered loudly.

At the end of the day, the principal gave a prize to the best class. We didn't win, but we got a certificate for the best food stall. We were very proud. I can't wait for the festival next year.

title: Learning to Swim
text:
When I was seven, I couldn't swim. I was afraid of the water. My mother decided that I needed lessons, so she took me to the swimming pool near our apartment.

The teacher was a tall man with a loud voice, but he was very patient. In the first lesson, I only sat at the side of the pool with my feet in the water. In the second lesson, I held a board and kicked my legs. The water went in my nose, and I cried a little.

After a month, I could swim from one side of the pool to the other. The teacher gave me a sticker with a picture of a fish on it. I put the sticker on the door of my room.

Now I am fifteen, and swimming is my favourite sport. I go to the pool three times a week. I am not afraid of the water anymore.

title: A Birthday Surprise
text:
Last week was my mother's birthday. My father, my brother, and I wanted to give her a surprise.

In the morning, my father took her to the market. While they were out, my brother and I cleaned the house. Then we made a cake. It was not a perfect cake. The top was a little burnt, and the cream was too soft. But we put strawberries on it, and it looked nice.

We also made a card. My brother drew a picture of the family, and I wrote a short poem inside.

When my mother came home, we turned off the lights. Then we sang "Happy Birthday" and brought out the cake with a candle on top. My mother was surprised. She laughed and said it was the best cake in the world. I don't think that is true, but it was a very happy evening.

title: The Weekend Market
text:
Every Sunday, there is a market in the square near my house. People come from all over the city to buy fresh food and other things.

The market opens at eight o'clock. When I arrive, the farmers are already selling fruit and vegetables. There is an old woman who sells honey. She always gives me a small spoon of honey to taste. There is also a man who sells fish. His fish is fresh because he catches it in the morning.

My favourite stall sells second-hand books. I usually spend an hour there. Last week I found a book about the history of the city for only two thousand won.

At the end of the market, I buy a bag of oranges and a bunch of flowers for my mother. Then I walk home slowly. The market is the best part of my week.

title: A Snowy Morning
text:
When I woke up this morning, the room was very cold. I looked out of the window, and everything was white. It snowed a lot in the night.

I put on a warm coat, a hat, and a pair of gloves. Then I went outside with my little brother. The snow was deep, and our boots made a funny sound. We made a snowman in the garden. My brother gave it a carrot for a nose and two stones for eyes. I put an old scarf around its neck.

Then our neighbour came out of his house. He had a big shovel, and he cleaned the snow from the road. We helped him for a while. After that, we had a snowball fight with the children next door.

When we came back inside, our hands were red. My mother made us a cup of hot chocolate. It was a perfect winter morning.

title: My Favourite Teacher
text:
My favourite teacher is Mr. Park. He teaches English at my middle school. He is a young teacher with short hair and glasses.

Mr. Park's classes are never boring. He often brings a song or a short video to class. Sometimes we play a game, and the winning team gets a sticker. Once, he wore a costume and pretended to be a famous writer. We all laughed, but we learned a lot about the writer's life.

Mr. Park is also very kind. When I had a problem with my homework, he stayed after school and helped me. He told me that making a mistake is an important part of learning.

Before I met Mr. Park, I didn't like English. Now it is my favourite subject. I want to be an English teacher like him in the future.

title: Camping by the Lake
text:
In August, my family went camping by a lake in the mountains. We drove for three hours to get there.

When we arrived, my father and I put up the tent. It was not easy, and it took a long time. My mother and sister collected wood for a fire. In the evening, we cooked sausages over the fire and ate them with bread.

After dinner, it was very dark. There were no lights, so we could see a lot of stars in the sky. My father showed us the moon through a small telescope. Then we heard an owl in a tree near the tent. My sister was scared, but I thought it was exciting.

In the morning, we went swimming in the lake. The water was clear and cold. It was the best holiday we had this year.

title: A Visit to the Doctor
text:
Last Tuesday, I woke up with a bad cold. I had a headache and a sore throat, so I didn't go to school. My mother took me to the doctor.

The waiting room was full of people. A baby was crying, and an old man was reading a newspaper. We waited for about half an hour. Then a nurse called my name.

The doctor was a friendly woman. She looked at my throat and listened to my chest. She said it was only a cold, and I needed to rest. She gave me a prescription for some medicine.

After the visit, we went to the pharmacy next to the hospital. The pharmacist gave me the medicine and told me to take it after every meal. When we got home, I went to bed and slept for the whole afternoon. The next day, I felt a lot better.

title: Moving to a New City
text:
Last year, my father got a new job in Daejeon, so my family moved there from Seoul. At first, I was not happy about it. I didn't want to leave my friends, my school, or the little park near our apartment.

The day we moved was very busy. A big truck came in the morning, and two men carried our furniture down the stairs. My mother packed the kitchen things in a box, and I packed my books and clothes. It took the whole day to drive to the new city, and we arrived late at night.

Our new home is an apartment on the tenth floor. From the window, I can see a river and a mountain. My room is bigger than my old room, and it has a desk by the window.

The first day at my new school was difficult. I didn't know anyone, and I sat alone at lunch. But on the second day, a boy named Jisu asked me to play soccer with his friends. He is now my best friend. We go to the same English academy, and we often ride our bikes along the river after class.

I still miss Seoul sometimes. I talk to my old friends on the phone, and in the summer one of them came to visit me. We went to a science museum and ate at a restaurant that sells the best noodles in the city.

Now, after a year, I like my new life. The city is quieter than Seoul, and the air is cleaner. I learned that a change can be scary, but it can also be a good thing.

title: The Little Restaurant
text:
My uncle has a small restaurant in the centre of town. It is not a famous restaurant, but the people in the neighbourhood love it. He opened it ten years ago, and he works there every day except Monday.

The restaurant has only six tables. On the wall, there is a painting of the sea and a clock that is always five minutes slow. In the corner, there is an old radio that plays music all day.

My uncle makes the food himself. His most popular dish is a spicy chicken soup. He uses a recipe from his mother, and he says it is a secret. Many customers come every week just for the soup. He also makes an excellent kimchi pancake.

During the summer holiday, I helped my uncle in the restaurant. I washed the dishes, cleaned the tables, and carried the food to the customers. It was hard work. My feet hurt at the end of the day, and once I dropped a plate on the floor. My uncle only laughed and gave me a broom.

I learned a lot that summer. I learned how to cut vegetables quickly and how to talk to customers politely. I also learned that running a restaurant is not easy. My uncle gets up at five o'clock every morning to buy fish and vegetables at the market. He goes home at ten o'clock at night.

At the end of the summer, my uncle gave me an envelope with some money in it. He also gave me a card that said, "Thank you for your help. You are always welcome in my kitchen." I keep the card in a drawer in my desk. One day, I want to have a restaurant of my own.

title: The Robot Competition
text:
This year, our science club entered a robot competition. There were four of us in the team: me, Hana, Junho, and Yuri. Our teacher, Ms. Kim, helped us after school.

The rules were simple. Each team had to build a robot that could carry a ball from one side of a table to the other. The robot that did it in the shortest time was the winner.

We worked on the robot for two months. Junho was good at building, so he made the body of the robot. Hana and I wrote the program on a laptop. Yuri designed a small arm to hold the ball. We had a lot of problems. The robot often turned in the wrong direction, and once the arm fell off. Every time something went wrong, we stayed late and tried again.

The competition was in a big hall at the university. There were thirty teams from all over the country. Some of the robots looked very expensive. When we saw them, we felt nervous.

In the first round, our robot dropped the ball. We had only one more chance. Before the second round, Hana changed a number in the program. This time, the robot picked up the ball and carried it across the table in eleven seconds. The audience clapped loudly.

We didn't win the competition. A team from Busan won with a time of eight seconds. But we finished in fifth place, and the judges gave us a special prize for teamwork. Ms. Kim took a photo of us with the prize, and the photo is now on the wall of our classroom.

Next year, we want to build an even better robot.

title: A Trip to Jeju Island
text:
In the spring, my family took a trip to Jeju Island. It was my first time on an airplane, so I was very excited. The flight from Seoul was only an hour long. From the window, I could see the sea and some small islands.

When we arrived, my father rented a car at the airport. We drove to a hotel near the beach. Our room had a balcony, and in the morning we could hear the waves.

On the first day, we climbed a mountain called Seongsan Ilchulbong. The path was steep, and it took about thirty minutes to reach the top. My little brother complained the whole way, but the view was amazing. We could see the ocean on every side.

On the second day, we visited a farm where they grow tangerines. The farmer gave each of us a basket, and we picked the fruit from the trees. The tangerines were small and very sweet. We also bought a box to take home to our grandparents.

In the evening, we went to a market and tried a lot of local food. My favourite was the grilled black pork. My mother liked the seafood, and my brother ate three pieces of a tangerine cake.

On the last day, it rained, so we went to a museum. It was a museum about the women divers of Jeju, who are called haenyeo. They dive into the cold sea without any air tanks to catch shellfish. I was surprised that some of the divers are more than seventy years old.

The trip was short, but it was one of the best holidays I have ever had. I hope we can go back to the island again soon.

title: The Old Photograph
text:
One day, while I was cleaning my room, I found an old photograph in a box under the bed. It was a black and white photo of a young man standing next to a bicycle. Behind him was a small shop with a sign above the door.

I didn't know the man, so I showed the photo to my mother. She smiled and said, "That is your grandfather. He was about twenty years old in that picture." I was very surprised. My grandfather is now an old man with white hair, and I couldn't believe it was the same person.

That weekend, I visited my grandfather and took the photo with me. When he saw it, his eyes became bright. He told me a long story about it.

When he was young, he worked in a shop that repaired bicycles. The owner of the shop was a kind man who taught him everything. My grandfather rode the bicycle in the photo to work every day, even in the snow. He saved his money for three years and bought the bicycle himself. It was the most expensive thing he had.

He also told me that he met my grandmother because of that bicycle. One day, her bicycle had a flat tyre, and she brought it to the shop. My grandfather fixed it, and he didn't ask her for any money. A week later, she came back with a box of cookies to say thank you.

I asked my grandfather if he still had the bicycle. He laughed and said no, it was lost a long time ago. But he still has the photograph now, because I gave it to him. He put it in a frame on the table next to his bed.

title: Volunteering at an Animal Shelter
text:
Last winter, I started volunteering at an animal shelter. The shelter is on the edge of the city, and it takes care of dogs and cats that don't have a home. I go there every Saturday morning with my friend Eunji.

When we arrive, we put on an apron and a pair of gloves. First, we clean the cages and give the animals fresh water. Then we feed them. The dogs are always very excited at breakfast time. They jump and bark until we put the food in their bowls.

After that, we take the dogs for a walk. There is a path along a river near the shelter. Some dogs walk slowly, but others pull hard on the lead. Eunji's favourite dog is a big brown dog named Bori. He is very strong, but he is also very gentle.

My favourite animal is a small grey cat with only one eye. The workers at the shelter call her Lucky. When she first came to the shelter, she was very thin and afraid of people. Now she sits on my lap and sleeps while I read a book to her.

Many people visit the shelter to adopt an animal. When an animal finds a new family, the workers ring a bell in the office. Everybody claps, and sometimes I cry a little because I am happy and sad at the same time.

Last month, a young couple adopted Lucky. I was sad to say goodbye, but I know she has a good home now. The couple sent a photo of her sleeping on their sofa. Volunteering at the shelter is hard work, but it is the most important thing I do every week.

title: A Day Without a Phone
text:
Our teacher gave us an unusual homework assignment. We had to spend a whole day without a phone, and then write about it. At first, I thought it would be easy. I was wrong.

On Saturday morning, I gave my phone to my mother. She put it in a drawer in the kitchen. Without it, I didn't know what time it was, so I looked for an old clock in the living room.

After breakfast, I wanted to check my messages. I walked to the kitchen three times before I remembered that my phone was in the drawer. I felt a little nervous. What if my friends were talking about something important?

At eleven o'clock, I was bored, so I went for a walk in the park. Usually I listen to music when I walk, but this time I listened to the birds and the wind in the trees. I saw an old man feeding pigeons and a family having a picnic on the grass. I never noticed these things before.

In the afternoon, I went to my friend's house. I didn't send a message first; I just knocked on the door. His mother was surprised, but she invited me in. We played a board game and talked for a long time. It was more fun than chatting online.

In the evening, I read a book for two hours. I finished the whole book, and I can't remember the last time I did that.

At the end of the day, my mother gave the phone back to me. I had forty messages, but none of them were important. In my homework, I wrote that a day without a phone was difficult, but it was also a nice change. I want to do it again once a month.

title: My Brother's Wedding
text:
Last month, my older brother got married. He is twenty-nine, and his wife, Jiyoung, is a nurse at a hospital in our city. They met at a friend's party three years ago.

The wedding was on a sunny Saturday in May. It was in a hotel in the centre of the city. In the morning, the whole family was very busy. My mother went to a salon to do her hair, and my father wore a new suit. I wore a dress that my aunt made for me.

The ceremony started at noon. My brother stood at the front of the hall in a black suit. He looked very nervous. Then the music started, and Jiyoung walked in with her father. She wore a long white dress, and everyone said she looked beautiful.

During the ceremony, my brother read a letter to Jiyoung. In the letter, he wrote about the first time they met. He said he spilled a glass of juice on her shoes. Everybody laughed, and Jiyoung laughed too.

After the ceremony, there was a big lunch for all the guests. There were more than two hundred people. We ate beef, noodles, and a lot of different salads. Then there was a traditional ceremony called pyebaek. My brother and Jiyoung wore hanbok and bowed to our parents and grandparents. My grandmother threw dates and chestnuts at them, and they tried to catch them in a cloth.

In the evening, the couple left for their honeymoon in Vietnam. The house is very quiet without my brother now. I miss him, but I am happy that he has a wonderful wife.

title: The School Trip to the Museum
text:
In November, our class went on a trip to the National Museum of Korea in Seoul. We left school at eight o'clock in the morning and travelled by bus. The trip took about an hour and a half.

The museum is a very large building with a beautiful garden in front of it. When we arrived, a guide met us at the entrance. She was a young woman with a soft voice. She gave each of us a small notebook and a pencil.

First, the guide took us to a room with very old things. There were stone tools and clay pots that were thousands of years old. The guide told us that people used the tools to cut meat and the pots to store food. It was hard to believe that people made them so long ago.

Next, we went to a room full of gold. There was a gold crown from the Silla Kingdom. It had many small pieces of jade on it, and it shone under the lights. My friend said it looked like a crown from a movie. The guide explained that only kings and queens wore crowns like this.

After lunch, we had some free time. I visited a room with paintings and a quiet, dark room with two bronze statues of a thinking figure. I sat on a bench and looked at the statues for a long time. It made me feel calm.

At the end of the visit, our teacher asked us to write about the most interesting thing we saw. I wrote about the gold crown. On the bus home, I looked at the pictures in my notebook. It was an interesting day, and I learned a lot about the history of my country.

title: Learning to Cook
text:
Until last year, I couldn't cook anything except instant noodles. When my mother started a new job, she often came home late, so I decided to learn to cook.

My first teacher was my grandmother. She showed me how to make rice in a pot and how to cut an onion without crying. She also taught me how to make a simple soup with tofu and vegetables. She said, "A good cook tastes the food many times." I still remember that.

At first, I made a lot of mistakes. Once, I put too much salt in the soup, and nobody could eat it. Another time, I forgot about the rice, and it burned. The smoke filled the kitchen, and the fire alarm went off. My little sister thought it was very funny.

After a few weeks, I started to get better. I watched videos online and tried a new recipe every weekend. I learned to make fried rice, an omelette, and a spicy stew with pork. My favourite dish was a pasta with tomato sauce. The recipe was from an Italian chef, and it was easier than I expected.

Now I cook dinner for my family three times a week. My mother is very happy because she can rest when she comes home. My father always asks for a second bowl, and my sister helps me wash the dishes.

Cooking is now one of my hobbies. I like going to the market and choosing fresh vegetables. I also like seeing my family enjoy the food that I make. Next year, I want to take a cooking class at a community centre. Maybe one day I will be a chef.

title: The Night Bus
text: When the last subway leaves, the night bus becomes the only way home for many people in the city. It is usually quiet on board. Some passengers sleep with their heads against the window, while others stare at their phones. The driver, an older man with a calm voice, greets everyone who gets on. For a lot of night workers, he is the first friendly face of the day.

title: A Message in a Bottle
text: While walking along the beach, a girl noticed a glass bottle half buried in the sand. Inside was a letter written in French. With the help of a translation app, she learned that a schoolboy had thrown the bottle into the sea eight years earlier. She decided to write back. A month later, she received a reply from the boy, who was now a university student.

title: Why We Yawn
text: Scientists still disagree about why we yawn. One popular theory is that a yawn helps to cool the brain, which may help us stay alert. Another idea is that yawning is a social signal. This could explain why yawning is so contagious. If you see a friend yawn, there is a good chance you will yawn too. Even reading about yawning can make some people do it.

title: The Corner Shop
text: For thirty years, an elderly couple ran the corner shop at the end of our street. They knew the name of every child in the neighbourhood. When the shop finally closed, the residents organised a farewell party in the car park. Somebody brought a cake shaped like the shop, and a local band played. The couple said it was the best evening of their lives.

title: Learning an Instrument as an Adult
text: Many people believe it is too late to learn an instrument after childhood. However, research suggests that adults can make excellent progress, especially if they practise regularly. An adult learner may not move as quickly as a child, but they often have a clearer goal and more patience. Practising for twenty minutes a day is usually more effective than practising for two hours once a week.

title: The Power Cut
text: The power went off just as we sat down for dinner. At first, there was a moment of complete silence. Then my father found a box of candles in the cupboard, and we ate by candlelight. Without the television, we talked for hours. My grandmother told us a story about the village she grew up in. When the lights came back on, nobody wanted to move.

title: Saving for a Goal
text: When I was fourteen, I wanted a guitar, but my parents said I had to pay for half of it. I made a plan. I put a jar on my desk and saved part of my allowance every week. I also washed the neighbour's car on Sundays. After eight months, I had enough money. The guitar is old now, but it is still the most valuable thing I own.

title: A Mistake at the Airport
text: On the way to a conference, a businessman realised that he had taken the wrong suitcase from the baggage belt. Inside was a wedding dress and a pair of silver shoes. He immediately called the airline. It turned out that the suitcase belonged to a bride who was getting married the next day. The airline sent a driver, and the dress arrived just in time for the ceremony.

title: Green Roofs
text: In many cities, architects are covering the roofs of buildings with plants. A green roof can reduce the temperature inside a building during the summer and help to absorb rainwater. It also provides a home for birds and insects. Although building a green roof is expensive at first, the owners often save money on energy in the long term. Some schools even use them as an outdoor classroom.

title: The Chess Club
text: Our school chess club started with only four members and a single old board. Today it has more than thirty members, and we meet every Thursday in the library. The club is open to everyone, from complete beginners to students who play in national tournaments. What I like most is that age doesn't matter. Last week, a first-year student beat the captain of the team.

title: The Benefits of Walking
text:
Walking is one of the simplest forms of exercise, but it has a surprising number of benefits. Unlike many sports, it doesn't require any special equipment, and almost anyone can do it.

Doctors say that a brisk walk of thirty minutes a day can lower the risk of heart disease and help to control weight. Walking also has a positive effect on mental health. Many people find that a walk in a park or along a river helps them to relax and think more clearly. Some writers and scientists have even said that their best ideas came to them while they were walking.

Another advantage is that walking can easily become part of a daily routine. Instead of taking the bus for a short journey, you can walk. Instead of using the lift, you can take the stairs. These small changes add up over time.

Of course, walking is not the answer to every health problem. However, for people who are looking for an easy way to become more active, it is an excellent place to start.

title: Working from Home
text:
In the past few years, the number of people who work from home has grown enormously. For some, it has been a positive change, while others have found it difficult.

One obvious benefit is that home workers don't have to commute. A person who used to spend an hour on a crowded train each morning now has extra time for sleep, exercise, or family. Many people also say that they can concentrate better without the noise of an office.

On the other hand, working from home can be lonely. Without colleagues around, it is easy to feel isolated. Some people also find it hard to separate work from the rest of their life. When the office is also the living room, it can be tempting to check emails late at night.

For this reason, many companies now offer a mixed system. Employees work in the office for part of the week and at home for the rest. This seems to be a sensible compromise, as it gives workers both flexibility and the chance to see their team in person.

title: The Story of the Sandwich
text:
According to a popular story, the sandwich is named after an English nobleman called the Earl of Sandwich, who lived in the eighteenth century. It is said that he loved playing cards so much that he didn't want to stop for a meal. Instead, he asked a servant to bring him a piece of meat between two slices of bread. That way, he could eat with one hand and continue playing with the other.

Historians are not sure whether this story is completely true. Some believe that the Earl actually ate this way while he was working at his desk. Either way, the name became popular, and soon people all over the country were asking for "the same as Sandwich."

Of course, the idea of putting food between pieces of bread is much older than the Earl. People in many cultures had eaten similar meals for centuries. However, it was in the eighteenth century that the sandwich got its name and became a fashionable snack.

Today, the sandwich is one of the most common lunches in the world, with an almost endless number of variations.

title: A Volunteer Firefighter
text:
In many rural areas, there aren't enough people to have a full-time fire service. Instead, local residents train as volunteer firefighters. My uncle has been one for twelve years.

During the day, he works as a mechanic in a small garage. But he always carries a pager, and when there is an emergency, he drops everything and drives to the fire station. He told me that he once left a customer's car with its engine still in pieces.

The training is not easy. Volunteers learn how to use the equipment, how to give first aid, and how to rescue people from a burning building. They also practise regularly, usually on a weekday evening.

My uncle says that the hardest part of the job is not the fire itself, but the waiting. When the pager goes off in the middle of the night, he never knows what he will find. Sometimes it is a small fire in a field. Other times, it is a serious accident on the motorway.

Despite the risks, he has no plans to stop. He believes that helping his community is a responsibility, not a hobby.

title: Why Do Leaves Change Colour?
text:
Every autumn, the leaves on many trees turn from green to brilliant shades of red, orange, and yellow. It is one of the most beautiful sights of the year, but what causes it?

During the spring and summer, leaves contain a large amount of a green substance called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll allows the tree to use sunlight to make food. It is so strong that it hides the other colours in the leaf.

As the days become shorter and the temperature drops, the tree stops producing chlorophyll. The green colour slowly disappears, and the yellow and orange colours that were there all along become visible. Some trees also produce a new red pigment in the autumn, which is why maple leaves can look so bright.

Eventually, the tree cuts off the supply of water to the leaves, and they fall to the ground. This helps the tree to save energy and water during the cold winter months. In the spring, the whole process begins again with a new set of leaves.

title: The First Day at a New Job
text:
I will never forget the first day at my first real job. I was hired as an assistant at a small design company, and I was so nervous that I arrived an hour early. The office was locked, so I waited in a café across the street and drank three cups of coffee.

When the manager finally arrived, she showed me around the office and introduced me to the team. There were only eight people, but I immediately forgot all of their names. She then gave me a laptop and asked me to prepare a presentation for a client meeting the next day.

I spent the whole afternoon working on it. At one point, I accidentally deleted the file and had to start again. By the time I finished, everyone else had gone home.

The next morning, I gave the presentation. My hands were shaking, but the client liked it, and the manager told me I had done a good job. On the way home, I felt tired but proud. I stayed at that company for five years, and I learned more there than anywhere else.

title: The Rise of Board Game Cafés
text:
Over the last decade, board game cafés have become popular in cities around the world. The idea is simple. Customers pay a small fee, order a drink or a snack, and choose from a library of hundreds of games.

For many people, these cafés offer a welcome break from screens. Instead of playing alone on a phone, friends sit around a table and talk, laugh, and argue about the rules. Some cafés employ a "game guru" who explains how each game works, so customers don't have to read a long instruction booklet.

The cafés are also popular with people who want to meet others. Many of them run events for singles or for people who are new to the city. A strategy game can be an easy way to start a conversation with a stranger.

Owners say that the most popular games are often the simplest ones. A quick card game that takes ten minutes to learn is usually more successful than a complicated game that takes an entire evening. Whatever the reason, it seems that people still enjoy the oldest kind of entertainment: playing together.

title: Kimchi and the Kimchi Fridge
text:
Kimchi is the most famous dish in Korean cuisine, and many families still make their own. Traditionally, kimchi was stored in large clay pots called onggi, which were buried in the ground during the winter. The soil kept the temperature low and stable, allowing the vegetables to ferment slowly.

As more people moved into apartments in the cities, burying a pot in the garden was no longer possible. An ordinary fridge was not a perfect solution either, because its temperature changed every time someone opened the door.

In the 1990s, Korean companies began to sell a special appliance called a kimchi refrigerator. It is designed to copy the conditions of an onggi under the ground. It keeps the temperature very stable and lets the owner control how quickly the kimchi ferments.

Today, a large number of Korean households have a kimchi fridge in addition to a normal one. Many people use it to store fruit, vegetables, and even rice as well. It is a good example of how a modern invention can help to keep an old tradition alive.

title: Lost in the Mountains
text:
Last October, my friend and I decided to climb a mountain that we had never visited before. The weather forecast said it would be sunny, so we didn't bring warm clothes. That was our first mistake.

The path was easy at first, but after about two hours, a thick fog came down. We couldn't see more than a few metres in front of us. At a fork in the path, we chose the left side. That was our second mistake.

After an hour of walking, we realised that we were completely lost. My phone had no signal, and the battery was almost dead. It was getting dark, and the temperature was dropping quickly.

Luckily, we heard the sound of a dog barking. We followed it and found a small farmhouse. An elderly farmer opened the door and invited us inside. His wife gave us a bowl of hot soup while he called the park office on his landline.

An hour later, a ranger arrived in a jeep and drove us back to the car park. Since that day, I always check the route carefully and pack a warm jacket, even when the sun is shining.

title: The Habit of Reading
text:
When I was a child, my parents read a story to me every night. As I got older, I started reading on my own, but in my teenage years, I stopped completely. My phone took up all of my free time.

Last year, I decided to change this. I set a simple goal: to read for fifteen minutes before going to sleep. At first, it was difficult. I kept reaching for my phone to check a message or watch a short video. So I started leaving the phone in the kitchen at night.

After a few weeks, fifteen minutes became thirty, and then an hour. I discovered that I was sleeping better, too. Reading a book seemed to calm my mind in a way that scrolling on a screen never did.

So far this year, I have read twenty-two books, from detective novels to a biography of a famous scientist. I have also joined a book club that meets once a month at a local café. Rediscovering reading has been one of the best decisions I have made, and the hardest part was simply getting started.

title: The Four-Day Working Week
text:
In recent years, a number of companies around the world have experimented with a four-day working week. Employees work for four days instead of five, but they receive the same salary. To many people, this sounds too good to be true. However, the results of several trials have been surprisingly positive.

Supporters of the idea argue that a shorter week makes workers happier and healthier. With an extra day off, people have more time to rest, exercise, and spend time with their families. As a result, they are less likely to suffer from stress and burnout. In some trials, the number of sick days fell significantly.

There is also evidence that productivity does not necessarily decrease. When employees know they have only four days to finish their work, they tend to focus better and waste less time. Many companies in the trials cut down on long meetings and unnecessary emails. Some managers reported that their teams produced the same amount of work, or even more, in less time.

However, the four-day week is not suitable for every kind of business. A hospital, for example, must be open every day, and a shop cannot simply close on Fridays. In these cases, a shorter week would mean hiring more staff, which increases costs. Critics also worry that some employees might try to fit five days of work into four, which could actually increase stress rather than reduce it.

Another challenge is fairness. If office workers enjoy a three-day weekend while factory workers do not, it could create tension within a company.

Despite these concerns, interest in the idea continues to grow. Several governments have funded trials, and some companies have made the change permanent after the trial ended. It is too early to say whether the four-day week will become the norm, but it has certainly started an important conversation about the way we work.

title: The Man Who Planted Trees
text:
On a river island in the north-east of India, there is a forest that did not exist forty years ago. It was planted, tree by tree, by one man. As a teenager, he saw a group of snakes that had died from the heat on a sandbank in the river, because there were no trees to give them shade. The sight shocked him, and he decided to do something about it.

He began by planting bamboo on the empty sandbank. Every day, he carried water from the river to the young plants. Many of them died, but he kept going. Over the years, he planted thousands of trees, including many different species. Slowly, the bare land turned into a forest.

As the forest grew, animals began to return. Birds built their nests in the trees, and deer and rabbits came to live there. Later, even a herd of elephants started to visit the forest every year. Tigers and rhinos have also been seen there.

For a long time, almost nobody knew about the forest. The man lived a simple life with his family, keeping cows and selling milk. It was only when a wildlife photographer came across the forest by chance that the story became known. Journalists from around the world came to interview him, and he received a national award for his work.

His story shows the remarkable difference that one person can make. He had no money, no machines, and no help from the government. He only had patience and a strong belief that the land could be saved.

Today, he still visits the forest every day and continues to plant new trees. When people ask him why he does it, his answer is simple. He says that trees give us life, and that if we protect nature, nature will protect us.

title: How Sleep Affects Learning
text:
Many students believe that the best way to prepare for an exam is to stay up all night studying. However, scientists who study the brain say that this is one of the worst things a student can do. Sleep, it turns out, plays a vital role in learning and memory.

During the day, the brain takes in a huge amount of new information. Much of this information is stored temporarily in an area called the hippocampus. While we sleep, the brain replays the events of the day and moves important information to other parts of the brain, where it can be stored for the long term. Without enough sleep, this process does not happen properly, and much of what we learned may be lost.

In one well-known type of experiment, two groups of people learn a list of words or a new skill. One group then sleeps for a full night, while the other stays awake. When both groups are tested the next day, the group that slept usually remembers significantly more.

Sleep also affects our ability to concentrate. A tired student finds it harder to pay attention in class and makes more mistakes. Even a single night of poor sleep can reduce performance on a test.

So how much sleep do young people need? Most experts recommend that teenagers get between eight and ten hours a night. Unfortunately, many teenagers get far less, partly because of homework, after-school activities, and the use of phones late at night. The light from a screen can also make it harder to fall asleep.

The message from scientists is clear. If you want to do well in an exam, it is better to study in short sessions over several weeks and get a good night's sleep before the test. An all-night study session might feel productive, but it is likely to do more harm than good.

title: Hangeul: An Alphabet with a Birthday
text:
Most writing systems developed slowly over hundreds or even thousands of years. Hangeul, the Korean alphabet, is unusual because it was created on purpose, at a specific time, by a specific person. It was invented in the fifteenth century under the direction of King Sejong the Great, and it was announced to the public in 1446.

Before Hangeul, Koreans wrote using Chinese characters. The problem was that Chinese and Korean are very different languages, and learning thousands of characters took many years of study. As a result, only a small number of people, mostly from the upper class, could read and write. King Sejong wanted to create a writing system that ordinary people could learn quickly.

The alphabet that he and his scholars designed is remarkably logical. The shapes of the consonants are based on the position of the mouth and tongue when the sounds are made. For example, the letter for the "g" sound shows the back of the tongue touching the roof of the mouth. The vowels are built from three basic symbols representing the sky, the earth, and a human being.

Not everyone welcomed the new alphabet. Some scholars argued that using it would damage the relationship with China and lower the status of educated people. For several centuries, Chinese characters remained the official way of writing, and Hangeul was often seen as a script for women and children.

However, in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, Hangeul gradually became the main writing system of Korea. Today, almost every Korean adult can read and write. Every year on the ninth of October, South Koreans celebrate Hangeul Day, a national holiday dedicated to the alphabet. It may be one of the only writing systems in the world with its own birthday.

title: The Problem with Fast Fashion
text:
Every year, the fashion industry produces billions of items of clothing. Much of it is what experts call "fast fashion": cheap, trendy clothes that are designed to be worn only a few times before being thrown away. While fast fashion has made new clothes affordable for many people, it has also created serious problems.

The first problem is waste. Because the clothes are so cheap, many people buy more than they need. A large proportion of these items end up in landfill within a year or two. Many fabrics, such as polyester, are made from plastic and can take hundreds of years to break down.

The second problem is the effect on the environment during production. Growing cotton requires an enormous amount of water. It is often said that producing a single cotton T-shirt can use thousands of litres. In addition, the chemicals used to dye fabrics are sometimes released into rivers, polluting the water that local people depend on.

There are also concerns about working conditions. To keep prices low, many garments are made in factories where workers earn very little and work long hours. In some cases, the factories have been unsafe, leading to tragic accidents.

So what can consumers do? One solution is simply to buy less and to choose clothes that will last for a long time. Another is to buy second-hand clothes from a charity shop or an online market. Repairing a torn shirt or swapping clothes with friends can also make a difference.

Some fashion brands have started to respond to these concerns by using recycled materials and offering repair services. However, critics say that real change will only happen when people's attitude towards clothing changes. As one campaigner put it, the most sustainable item of clothing is the one that is already in your wardrobe.

title: A Year Abroad
text:
When I was nineteen, I spent a year studying at a university in Canada. Before I left, I was excited but also very worried. My English was not perfect, I had never lived away from my family, and I didn't know a single person in the country.

The first few weeks were the hardest. I lived in a dormitory with a roommate from Brazil, and we communicated mostly through gestures and a translation app. In class, the professors spoke very quickly, and I understood only about half of what they said. I spent my evenings reading the textbook again and again, trying to catch up.

Things started to change when I joined the university hiking club. Every weekend, the club organised a trip to a lake or a mountain outside the city. At first, I was too shy to speak, but it is hard to stay silent when you are walking for six hours with a group of people. Slowly, I made friends, and my English improved much faster than it had in the classroom.

Living abroad also taught me to be independent. For the first time, I had to cook my own meals, manage my money, and solve problems without calling my parents. Once, I lost my wallet on the bus and had to cancel my bank card and replace my student ID on my own. It was stressful, but I felt proud when I had sorted everything out.

The winter was a shock. The temperature sometimes fell to minus thirty degrees, and the snow stayed on the ground for months. My Brazilian roommate had never seen snow before, and on the first snowy morning, he ran outside in his pyjamas.

When the year ended, I was surprised by how sad I felt. I had arrived as a nervous student and left as a more confident person. I still keep in touch with many of the friends I made, and my roommate visited me in Korea last summer.

title: The Honeybee Crisis
text:
Honeybees are small, but they play an enormous role in our lives. As they fly from flower to flower collecting nectar, they carry pollen from one plant to another. This process, known as pollination, allows many plants to produce fruit and seeds. It is estimated that around a third of the food we eat depends, at least in part, on pollinators such as bees.

In recent decades, however, beekeepers in many countries have reported large losses of bees. In some years, a significant proportion of colonies have died over the winter. Scientists have been trying to understand why.

There seems to be no single cause. One major factor is the use of certain pesticides, which can harm the bees' ability to find their way back to the hive. Another is a tiny parasite called the varroa mite, which attacks bees and spreads disease. Habitat loss is also important. As fields of wildflowers are replaced by roads, buildings, and huge farms growing a single crop, bees find it harder to get the variety of food they need.

Climate change may make the problem worse. Warmer temperatures can cause flowers to bloom earlier in the year, before bees are active, or allow new diseases to spread.

The good news is that there are many ways to help. Some countries have restricted the use of the pesticides that are most harmful to bees. Farmers are being encouraged to leave strips of wildflowers around their fields. In cities, people are setting up hives on rooftops and planting flowers on their balconies.

Even individuals can make a difference. Planting a variety of flowers, avoiding chemical sprays in the garden, and buying honey from local beekeepers are all simple steps. Protecting bees is not only about saving an insect; it is about protecting the food supply for future generations.

title: The Orchestra of Recycled Instruments
text:
In a small town in Paraguay, a community grew up beside a huge landfill site. Many families earned a living by collecting and selling rubbish. There was little money for anything else, and certainly not for musical instruments. A violin, for example, could cost more than a family's house.

A local music teacher had an idea. Together with a rubbish collector who was skilled at making things, he began to build instruments out of the waste from the landfill. They made violins from old oil cans and pieces of wood. A cello was made from a metal barrel, and the keys of a saxophone were made from bottle caps and coins. The instruments looked unusual, but the sound they produced was surprisingly good.

The teacher started to give lessons to the children of the community. For many of them, it was the first time they had ever had the chance to learn music. Practice gave them a reason to stay in school and a safe place to spend their afternoons.

Over the years, the group became an orchestra. A documentary film about them was made, and the orchestra began to receive invitations from abroad. The children, some of whom had never left their town, performed on stages in many countries, playing classical music as well as popular songs.

The orchestra has become a symbol of what creativity can achieve. It shows that talent exists everywhere, even in the poorest places, and that what many people see as rubbish can be turned into something beautiful.

The teacher often says that the world sends them its garbage, and they send back music. His words are a reminder that the value of something often depends on how we choose to look at it.

title: Should Homework Be Banned?
text:
Homework has been a part of school life for generations, but in recent years, some teachers and parents have begun to question whether it is really necessary. A few schools have even decided to stop giving homework altogether, especially to younger children. The debate is a lively one, with strong arguments on both sides.

Supporters of homework say that it helps students to practise what they have learned in class. A maths lesson, for example, may introduce a new skill, but students need to use it many times before they can do it confidently. Homework also teaches students to manage their time and to work independently, skills that will be important at university and in their future careers. In addition, it gives parents a chance to see what their children are studying.

Critics, however, argue that too much homework can do more harm than good. Many students already spend a long day at school, followed by extra classes in the evening. When they finally get home, they are tired, and a large pile of homework can cause stress and take away time for sleep, exercise, and family. Some research suggests that for young children in particular, homework has little effect on how well they do at school.

There is also the question of fairness. Some students have a quiet room, a computer, and parents who can help them. Others have none of these things. Homework may therefore increase the gap between students from different backgrounds.

Perhaps the answer lies somewhere in the middle. Many educators now believe that the quality of homework is more important than the quantity. A short, interesting task that encourages students to think, read, or explore a topic may be far more valuable than a long list of repetitive exercises. What is clear is that the purpose of homework should be to support learning, not simply to fill time.

title: The Lighthouse Keeper
text:
For more than two hundred years, a lighthouse has stood on a rocky island off the coast. For much of that time, it was looked after by a lighthouse keeper who lived there with his family. Today, the light is automatic, and the island is empty except for the seabirds. But the last keeper still remembers what life was like.

He arrived on the island as a young man with his wife and their newborn daughter. There was no electricity at first, and the lamp at the top of the tower had to be lit every evening and kept burning until dawn. Every few hours during the night, he climbed the narrow stairs to check the light and wind the mechanism that made it turn.

Life on the island was simple but demanding. A supply boat came once every two weeks, bringing food, letters, and fuel. In the winter, storms sometimes prevented the boat from coming for a month or more. The family grew vegetables in a small garden protected by a stone wall, and they caught fish from the rocks.

The keeper's most important job was to warn ships of danger. On foggy nights, when the light could not be seen, he sounded a loud horn every thirty seconds. On one occasion, he saw a fishing boat in trouble during a storm. He sent a radio message to the coast, and a rescue team was able to save the crew.

His daughter grew up on the island and went to school by correspondence, sending her homework to the mainland by boat. She says it was a lonely childhood in some ways, but also a magical one. She knew the name of every bird and could read the weather from the colour of the sky.

When the lighthouse was automated, the family had to leave. The keeper says it was one of the saddest days of his life. He still visits the island once a year, and every time he sees the light shining across the sea, he feels as if a part of him is still there.

title: The Placebo Effect
text: The placebo effect is one of the most puzzling phenomena in medicine. When patients are given a sugar pill that they believe to be a genuine treatment, a surprising number report an improvement in their symptoms. More remarkably, some studies suggest that the effect can persist even when patients are told that the pill contains no active ingredient. The expectation of relief, it seems, can be a powerful medicine in itself.

title: The Paradox of Choice
text: It seems logical that having more options should make us happier. However, a number of psychologists argue that an abundance of choice can be paralysing. Faced with dozens of almost identical products on a supermarket shelf, a shopper may struggle to decide, or may leave without buying anything at all. Even after making a choice, people often feel a nagging suspicion that a better alternative was available.

title: Urban Heat Islands
text: On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island effect, occurs because asphalt and concrete absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night. The lack of vegetation makes the problem worse, as trees provide shade and cool the air through the evaporation of water from their leaves.

title: The Last Speaker
text: When the last fluent speaker of a language dies, a unique way of understanding the world disappears with them. Linguists estimate that a significant proportion of the world's languages are endangered, many of them spoken only by a handful of elderly people. A language is not merely a set of words; it is a store of knowledge about local plants, history, and relationships that often cannot be translated precisely.

title: The Dunning-Kruger Effect
text: The Dunning-Kruger effect describes a cognitive bias in which people with limited knowledge of a subject tend to overestimate their own competence. The irony is that the skills needed to perform a task well are often the same skills needed to recognise a good performance. Consequently, a beginner may be blissfully unaware of their mistakes, while an expert is acutely conscious of how much they still have to learn.

title: Sourdough
text: Long before the invention of commercial yeast, bakers relied on a living culture known as a sourdough starter. The starter is simply a mixture of flour and water, colonised by wild yeasts and bacteria from the environment. Bakers feed it regularly, and some starters have reportedly been kept alive for over a century. The bacteria produce acids that give the bread its characteristic tangy flavour and help it to stay fresh for longer.

title: The Overview Effect
text: Many astronauts describe a profound shift in perspective after seeing the Earth from space. The planet appears as a fragile blue sphere suspended in darkness, with no visible borders between nations. This experience, which a writer named the overview effect, has led some astronauts to become passionate advocates for environmental protection and international cooperation, convinced that humanity shares a single, vulnerable home.

title: A Forgotten Inventor
text: History tends to remember the person who popularised an invention rather than the one who first conceived it. In many cases, an idea emerged in several places at roughly the same time, and the credit went to whoever secured a patent or attracted the attention of the press. The story of an invention is therefore rarely the story of a lone genius, but rather of a gradual, collective process.

title: Microplastics
text: Microplastics are fragments of plastic smaller than five millimetres. They are produced when larger items break down, but they also come from synthetic clothing, car tyres, and some cosmetics. Researchers have detected them in the deepest ocean trenches, in Arctic snow, and in the human bloodstream. The long-term effects on health remain unclear, which has prompted calls for a more cautious approach to plastic production.

title: Why We Procrastinate
text: Procrastination is often dismissed as a sign of laziness or poor time management. Psychologists, however, increasingly regard it as an emotional problem rather than a practical one. People tend to postpone a task not because they lack the time, but because the task provokes an unpleasant feeling, such as boredom, anxiety, or a fear of failure. Avoiding it brings temporary relief, which unfortunately reinforces the habit.

title: The Ethics of Self-Driving Cars
text:
As self-driving cars move closer to becoming an everyday reality, engineers face a question that was once confined to philosophy classrooms. If an accident is unavoidable, how should the car decide whom to protect?

The dilemma resembles a famous thought experiment known as the trolley problem, in which a person must choose whether to divert a runaway train so that it kills one person instead of five. In the case of an autonomous vehicle, the decision would not be made in a moment of panic, but programmed in advance by a team of developers.

Surveys conducted across many countries have revealed that people's intuitions vary considerably. Most respondents believe that a car should minimise the total number of casualties, yet many also admit that they would be reluctant to buy a car that might sacrifice its own passengers.

Some experts argue that the debate is a distraction. Since the vast majority of road accidents are caused by human error, they contend, the overriding priority should be to make autonomous vehicles as safe as possible, rather than to solve every hypothetical scenario.

title: The Invention of Time Zones
text:
Until the nineteenth century, most towns set their clocks according to the position of the sun. Noon was simply the moment when the sun was highest in the sky, which meant that a town a short distance to the west would be several minutes behind its neighbour. For most of human history, this caused little inconvenience.

The arrival of the railway changed everything. A train travelling across a country would pass through dozens of local times, making it almost impossible to publish a coherent timetable. Railway companies began to adopt a standard time along their lines, and confusion arose wherever different companies used different clocks.

In 1884, delegates from around the world gathered in Washington for a conference that established the meridian passing through Greenwich, in London, as the starting point for measuring longitude. This paved the way for a global system of time zones, each roughly fifteen degrees wide.

Even today, however, time zones are as much a political matter as a geographical one. Some countries span an enormous distance yet observe a single time, while others have adopted offsets of half an hour or even forty-five minutes.

title: The Science of Expertise
text:
It is often claimed that it takes ten thousand hours of practice to master a skill. The figure became popular after it appeared in a bestselling book, which drew on research into the training habits of elite violinists. The idea is appealing because it suggests that excellence is within the reach of anyone who is willing to work hard enough.

The researchers behind the original study, however, have since pointed out that the number was never intended as a fixed rule. The amount of practice required varies enormously from one field to another, and from one individual to the next.

More importantly, they emphasised that the type of practice matters far more than the quantity. What they called deliberate practice involves working at the edge of one's ability, receiving immediate feedback, and focusing on specific weaknesses. Simply repeating a task that one can already perform comfortably produces little improvement, no matter how many hours are spent on it.

This distinction helps to explain why many people who have driven a car for decades are not noticeably better drivers than they were after their first year. Experience, in other words, is not the same as expertise.

title: The Rosetta Stone
text:
In 1799, soldiers in Napoleon's army discovered a slab of dark stone near the town of Rashid, known to Europeans as Rosetta, in the Nile Delta. The stone was inscribed with the same decree written in three different scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs, a cursive Egyptian script known as Demotic, and ancient Greek.

At the time, nobody had been able to read hieroglyphs for well over a thousand years. Because scholars could understand the Greek text, the stone offered a unique opportunity to unlock the meaning of the other two scripts.

The breakthrough came gradually. An English scholar, Thomas Young, made important early progress, recognising that certain groups of symbols enclosed in an oval represented the names of royalty. However, it was the French linguist Jean-François Champollion who, in 1822, demonstrated that hieroglyphs combined phonetic signs with symbols representing whole words or ideas. His knowledge of Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language, proved crucial.

The decipherment opened up thousands of years of Egyptian history to modern readers. Today, the stone is displayed in the British Museum, although its location remains a subject of debate, and there have been calls for it to be returned to Egypt.

title: Behavioural Nudges
text:
Governments have traditionally tried to influence behaviour through laws, taxes, and information campaigns. In recent decades, however, many have turned to a subtler approach known as nudging. A nudge is a small change in the way choices are presented that makes a desirable option more likely, without forbidding any alternative.

A frequently cited example concerns pension savings. When employees must actively sign up for a retirement scheme, a large proportion never get around to doing so. When enrolment is automatic and employees must opt out if they do not wish to participate, participation rates rise dramatically, even though the choice available is exactly the same.

Other nudges include placing fruit at eye level in a school canteen or sending a letter informing people that most of their neighbours have already paid their taxes.

Critics have raised concerns about the approach. Some argue that nudges are a form of manipulation, steering people's decisions without their full awareness. Others question whether a policy that relies on minor psychological tricks can tackle complex social problems. Supporters respond that every choice is presented in some way, so the real question is not whether to influence people, but how to do so responsibly.

title: The Hidden Cost of Free Apps
text:
Most of the applications on a typical smartphone cost nothing to download. Social networks, search engines, and many games are offered free of charge to billions of users. Yet the companies behind them are among the most valuable in the world. How is this possible?

The answer lies in data. As we scroll, search, and click, these platforms collect a detailed record of our behaviour: what we read, where we go, whom we communicate with, and how long we look at a particular image. This information allows advertisers to target an audience with remarkable precision, and they are prepared to pay a considerable premium for it.

The arrangement has been summarised in a well-known phrase: if you are not paying for the product, you are the product. Although this is perhaps an oversimplification, it captures an important truth about the digital economy.

In response to growing concerns about privacy, several governments have introduced legislation requiring companies to explain how they use personal data and to obtain the consent of users. Critics argue, however, that few people actually read the lengthy terms and conditions they agree to, which makes the notion of informed consent somewhat questionable.

title: The Rise and Fall of the Dodo
text:
The dodo was a large, flightless bird that lived on the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. Having evolved in the absence of predators, it had no reason to fear humans when Dutch sailors arrived at the end of the sixteenth century. Within less than a century, the species had vanished entirely.

For a long time, the dodo was portrayed as a clumsy, foolish creature that was somehow destined for extinction. Recent research has challenged this image. Analysis of skeletons suggests that the bird was more agile than previously believed, and that the overweight figures depicted in many early paintings may have been based on overfed captive specimens.

Hunting by sailors was only part of the story. The animals that humans brought to the island, including pigs, rats, and monkeys, probably did even greater damage by destroying nests and eating eggs. The destruction of the forest habitat also played a role.

Today, the phrase "as dead as a dodo" is used to describe something that is completely obsolete. The bird has also become a powerful symbol of the impact that humans can have on fragile ecosystems, and a reminder of how quickly a species can be lost.

title: Translation and Untranslatable Words
text:
Every language contains words that seem to resist translation. Korean, for example, has the word "jeong," which refers to a deep sense of attachment and affection that develops over time between people, or even between a person and a place. English has no single equivalent, and a translator must choose between an awkward explanation and an approximation that loses much of the nuance.

Such words are often presented as evidence that speakers of different languages think in fundamentally different ways. The reality is more complicated. The absence of a single word does not mean that a concept is unknown; English speakers can certainly experience the feeling that "jeong" describes, even if they need a whole sentence to express it.

Nevertheless, the vocabulary of a language does reveal something about the priorities of a culture. A concept that is important enough to deserve its own word is likely to be discussed frequently and to shape the way people interpret their experiences.

For translators, the challenge is not simply to find matching words, but to convey the meaning, tone, and cultural associations of the original text. It is an art as much as a science, and a skilled translator is in many ways a co-author of the work.

title: The Psychology of Queues
text:
Waiting in a queue is one of the most universally disliked experiences of modern life. Interestingly, research suggests that our frustration often depends less on the actual length of the wait than on how the wait is perceived.

One well-known principle is that unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time. This is why many hotels place a mirror beside the lifts and why some airports deliberately make the walk to the baggage area longer: passengers who are walking feel that they are making progress, whereas those standing at an empty carousel grow impatient.

Uncertainty also makes waiting more stressful. A display that tells customers how many minutes remain can significantly reduce anxiety, even if it does not shorten the wait at all. Similarly, people are far more tolerant of a delay when they are given an explanation for it.

Perhaps most importantly, people care deeply about fairness. A single line that serves customers in order of arrival is often preferred to several parallel lines, even when the average wait is identical, because nobody has to suffer the indignity of watching a neighbouring queue move faster.

title: The Secret Life of Fungi
text:
When we think of fungi, we usually picture a mushroom. Yet the mushroom is merely the fruiting body of an organism that lives largely out of sight. Beneath the surface of the soil, most fungi consist of a vast network of microscopic threads called hyphae, which can extend over an enormous area.

Many of these networks form a partnership with the roots of plants. The fungus supplies the plant with water and minerals that it has extracted from the soil, and in return, the plant provides the fungus with sugars produced through photosynthesis. The vast majority of plant species are thought to depend on such relationships.

Some researchers have suggested that these networks also allow trees to exchange resources and even chemical signals, a concept popularly described as the "wood wide web." The idea has captured the public imagination, although other scientists caution that the evidence for widespread cooperation between trees remains limited and that the metaphor may be overstated.

What is beyond dispute is that fungi are essential to life on land. By breaking down dead material, they recycle nutrients and keep ecosystems functioning. Without them, the forest floor would soon be buried under a thick layer of fallen leaves and wood.

title: The Attention Economy
text:
In an age of information abundance, the scarcest resource is no longer knowledge but attention. This insight, first articulated by economists several decades ago, has become the foundation of what is now called the attention economy. Technology companies compete not primarily for our money, but for our time, since the longer we remain on a platform, the more advertisements we see and the more data we generate.

To capture and hold our attention, designers employ a range of techniques drawn from behavioural psychology. The infinite scroll removes the natural stopping point that a page or a chapter once provided. Notifications arrive at unpredictable intervals, exploiting the same mechanism of variable reward that makes slot machines so compelling. Even the colour of an alert badge is chosen to trigger a sense of urgency.

The consequences of this competition are a subject of intense debate. Some researchers have linked heavy use of social media to anxiety, poor sleep, and difficulty concentrating, particularly among adolescents. Others caution that the evidence is mixed and that correlation should not be mistaken for causation; it may be that people who are already unhappy are more likely to spend long hours online.

What is less disputed is that the business model creates a conflict of interest. A platform that profits from engagement has little incentive to encourage users to log off, even when doing so would be in their best interest. Content that provokes outrage or fear tends to spread faster than calm, balanced information, and algorithms designed to maximise engagement may therefore amplify divisive material.

In response, a growing movement advocates what is sometimes called humane technology. Its supporters argue that devices and apps should be designed to respect users' time and well-being rather than to exploit their vulnerabilities. Some practical suggestions include turning off non-essential notifications, setting the screen to greyscale, and keeping phones out of the bedroom.

Ultimately, the question is not whether technology is good or bad, but who controls it. If we do not decide how to spend our attention, someone else will happily decide for us.

title: The Discovery of Penicillin
text:
The story of penicillin is often told as a tale of happy accident. In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned to his laboratory in London after a holiday and noticed that a mould had contaminated one of his dishes of bacteria. Around the mould was a clear zone where the bacteria had been destroyed. Fleming identified the mould as a species of Penicillium and named the active substance penicillin.

Yet the popular version of the story leaves out a great deal. Fleming published his findings, but he struggled to purify the substance or produce it in useful quantities, and for about a decade his discovery attracted relatively little attention. Many scientists doubted that it could survive long enough in the human body to be effective.

The real transformation began at the end of the 1930s, when a team at the University of Oxford, led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, took up the research. Working with very limited resources, they developed methods to extract and purify penicillin. One member of the team, Norman Heatley, devised an ingenious system for producing the mould in large containers, including bedpans adapted for the purpose.

In 1941, the team treated their first human patient, a police officer who was suffering from a severe infection. He improved dramatically, but the supply of penicillin ran out before he could be cured, and he eventually died. The case nevertheless demonstrated the drug's extraordinary potential.

With Britain at war, large-scale production moved to the United States, where researchers discovered a more productive strain of the mould on a rotting melon bought at a market. By the end of the Second World War, penicillin was being manufactured in vast quantities and had saved countless lives.

In 1945, Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Fleming himself warned in his acceptance lecture that the misuse of penicillin could lead to resistant bacteria, a prediction that has proved alarmingly accurate. Today, antibiotic resistance is regarded as one of the most serious threats to global health.

title: The Case for Boredom
text:
Boredom has a poor reputation. It is generally regarded as an unpleasant state to be avoided at all costs, and modern technology has made it easier than ever to do so. At the first hint of tedium, whether in a queue, on a train, or during an advertisement break, most of us instinctively reach for a phone. Yet a growing body of research suggests that we may be depriving ourselves of something valuable.

Psychologists define boredom as the uncomfortable feeling of wanting to engage in a satisfying activity but being unable to do so. Crucially, it functions as a signal. Much like hunger tells us that we need food, boredom tells us that our current situation is not meeting our needs, and it motivates us to seek something more meaningful.

Several studies have explored the link between boredom and creativity.
